description: Hello! This team focuses on constructing and highly specialized landing system for lunar landers.
summary: FHLS is a website that lets you click anywhere on the Moon and see, hour by hour throughout 2027 and 2028, how much sunlight it gets and how often it faces Earth for comms. It uses real data from LOLA and NASA’s SPICE module to build a 3D model of the Moon. It simplifies the data for students, sparks curiosity in hobbyists and provides aid for mission planners. This is especially important because, for the first time in over 50 years, astronauts are planned to land on the Moon, this time at the south pole, a place with rocky terrain where a single peak can block sunlight for days.
details:
Artemis IV is planned to land at the south pole, where the Sun only stays 1–2° above the horizon. On top of that, Earth wobbles around ±6.7° in the sky. That's why a tiny miscalculation, or one ridge, can block sunlight or comms with Earth for days. We acknowledge there is a lot of software built for this, but most of it is aimed at experts, it is hard to test quickly, and it doesn't give a surface-level understanding.

Our project features a 3D Moon built with terrain from real NASA data gathered by LOLA, with Sun and Earth positions calculated using NASA's SPICE module. It uses three.js (WebGL) to generate the 3D model in the user's browser. You can zoom across and inspect real terrain.

Inspired by architects, we came up with a new approach to viewing things: the horizon panorama. It gives you a 360° look at the whole skyline around a spot, with the paths of the Sun and Earth in sight.

The software outputs the % of sunlight, the % of Earth contact, both, and the longest blackout (the detail depends on which mode you are in). Best landing dates and best landing sites are given, which could be key to developing an area. You can also pick an exact date and hour, step forward or back by an hour or a day, and jump straight to a best landing window. We also have a timeline to simulate going through 2027 to 2028, and you can select individual hours of that time. We added sunlight maps, with inspiration taken from heat maps, covering the whole Moon. On top of this, you are able to compare up to 3 sites to check which one suits your mission best.

We have built 3 modes:

Beginner:
Easy answers, like "about half the time", in plain words with a simple sentence. It tells you if the spot gets sunlight and if it can see Earth, with icons and no numbers to worry about. It's made for students and anyone curious, so you understand the spot in seconds.

Intermediate:
It gives the angles and the information that interests hobbyists: how high the Sun and Earth are, the percentages of time with sunlight, Earth contact and both, the windows on the timeline, and the horizon panorama with the Sun and Earth moving across the skyline. You see why a spot has power or not, not only the answer.

Advanced:
It has the full detail that can be useful to mission planners: exact numbers, exact UTC times, an hour-by-hour table, the exact start and end of the best landing windows, and a CSV export, so the data can be used in their own tools.

The difference between the 3 modes: all three use the same data. Beginner gives the answer, Intermediate shows how it works, and Advanced gives every number.

A key finding: Connecting Ridge and de Gerlache Rim 2 are both Artemis candidate sites located near the south pole. They are less than 50 km apart, yet Connecting Ridge's longest blackout is 21 days, while de Gerlache Rim 2's is 115 days.

We validated the data by comparing it with NASA's south polar illumination map (LOLA, PGDA). 400 random points were checked and showed a 0.99 correlation and a mean difference of 0.8 points. All 37 of 37 shadowed points agreed.

There are limits:

  • Just being able to see the Sun and Earth doesn't guarantee power and comms.
  • It is not a landing safety check: boulders, temperature and slope are not included.
  • Although the data is not affected, the 3D model has a bit less resolution away from the poles.

NASA data:

  • JPL NAIF SPICE (DE440, Moon orientation): https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/naif/data_generic.html (files used: de440s.bsp, moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc, moon_de440_250416.tf, naif0012.tls, pck00011.tpc)
  • LRO LOLA polar maps (40 m) and global maps: https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/missions/lro/lola.htm
  • LOLA illumination map (PGDA product 69), used for validation: https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/69
  • NASA CGI Moon Kit (globe textures): https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4720
  • Apollo 11 photo (AS11-40-5903, public domain): https://images.nasa.gov

Other resources: three.js, Open Sans font, Python (numpy, spiceypy)
Music: "Interstellar" by QuentinGaming (Pixabay)

Tools and languages: Python (numpy, spiceypy) for the data engine, JavaScript and three.js (WebGL) for the website, hosted on GitHub Pages.

Use of AI

  • Tools: Claude, Codex
  • Used for: code, checking, helping with drafting text
  • The validation animation, opening title and end card in our video were made with AI-written scripts from our own data.
  • Our team: the idea, the decisions, the validation, testing and reviewing everything
